summary: In Greek mythology, Amymone ("blameless; innocent") is one of the fifty Danaids, daughters of Danaus. Sent to find water when Poseidon had dried the springs of Argos, she met a satyr and then Poseidon, who revealed the springs of Lerna (or a spring named for her) and became by her the father of the seafarer Nauplius, eponym of Nauplia. Distinct from any naiad daughter of Inachus who shares the name.
etymology: Ancient Greek Ἀμυμώνη (Amymónē), "blameless" or "innocent"; her name has invited identification with Hypermnestra, the one Danaid who spared her husband.

sections.heading: Poseidon and the spring
paragraphs: After Inachus awarded Argos to Hera, Poseidon punished the land with drought. Danaus sent his daughters for water; Amymone, hunting or searching with a dart, roused a satyr who pursued her. Poseidon drove the satyr off, lay with Amymone, and showed her the Lernaean springs — or had her pull his lodged trident from a rock so that water gushed forth.

She bore Nauplius, the navigator who founded Nauplia on the Argive coast. Aeschylus wrote a lost satyr play Amymone on the seduction; Roman mosaics often show Poseidon approaching her with a water jug as her attribute.

sections.heading: Among the Danaids
paragraphs: Apollodorus lists her among Danaus's daughters by Europa and as wife of Enceladus, whom she slew on the wedding night with forty-eight sisters. Other strands treat her as the "blameless" Danaid who refused murder — overlapping Hypermnestra — and mother of Abas by Lynceus. Her pitcher recalls Lerna's waters and, by contrast, the leaky jars of the punished Danaids in Tartarus.
